candidates.title: Lipschitz-Constrained EEGNet: Formal Robustness Guarantees for EEG-Based BCIs
candidates.summary: This paper integrates Parseval tight frame constraints into EEGNet's convolutional layers to enforce a bounded Lipschitz constant, providing formal robustness guarantees against adversarial perturbations. The approach modifies EEGNet's training to maintain orthogonal weight matrices while preserving its EEG-specific feature extraction capabilities. Evaluations on BCI Competition IV P300, BNCI Horizon SMR, and MRCP datasets measure robustness via CLEVER scores, adversarial detection AUC, and accuracy under FGSM/PGD attacks, comparing against standard EEGNet, adversarially trained EEGNet, and Parseval-constrained EEGNet ablations.
candidates.gap: While ref-021 shows EEG-based BCIs can detect adversarial examples, no work provides formal Lipschitz-based robustness guarantees for EEGNet. Ref-005 and ref-020 establish Lipschitz bounds for general networks, but these have not been adapted to EEG-specific architectures like EEGNet, which require specialized depthwise separable convolutions.
candidates.approach: Modify EEGNet's convolutional layers to maintain Parseval tight frame constraints via orthogonal weight matrices during training. Input: raw EEG time-series; Output: class probabilities. Objective: minimize cross-entropy loss with orthogonal weight regularization. Update rule: project weight matrices onto Stiefel manifolds after each gradient step. Core difference: ref-010's Parseval networks use standard convolutions, while this work adapts them to EEGNet's depthwise separable convolutions and temporal filters.
candidates.evaluation: Evaluate on BCI Competition IV P300, BNCI Horizon SMR, and MRCP datasets. Baselines: standard EEGNet, adversarially trained EEGNet (ref-013), and Parseval-constrained EEGNet with only spatial filters modified. Measures: CLEVER scores (ref-009) with ε=0.1, adversarial detection AUC (ref-021) against FGSM/PGD, and accuracy under PGD attacks (20 steps, ε=0.1). Ablation: compare full model with version where only temporal filters are Parseval-constrained.

candidates.title: Ethical Robustness Verification for BCI Systems: Bridging Safety and Human Rights
candidates.summary: This paper introduces a framework for verifying BCI systems against adversarial threats while ensuring compliance with proposed neuro-rights (e.g., cognitive liberty, mental privacy). It formalizes robustness requirements as quadratic constraints and integrates them into a semidefinite programming (SDP) verification pipeline. The approach maps neuro-rights principles to specific SDP constraints, such as bounded input perturbations for private mental states, and evaluates the framework on EEG-based BCI models with sensitive data.
candidates.gap: Current SDP-based robustness verification (ref-005) does not explicitly model BCI-specific ethical constraints, such as mental privacy. While ref-016 defines neuro-rights (e.g., right to mental privacy), ref-017 shows that existing BCI security countermeasures do not formally enforce these rights through verifiable technical constraints.
candidates.approach: Extend ref-005's SDP framework by adding quadratic constraints derived from neuro-rights principles (e.g., bounded perturbations on EEG features linked to private mental states). The pipeline takes a trained BCI model (e.g., EEGNet from ref-001) and input uncertainty set, and outputs a certified robustness radius under ethical constraints. It differs from ref-005 by incorporating domain-specific constraints (e.g., bounded slope for ERN-related EEG channels) to enforce neuro-rights.
candidates.evaluation: Test the framework on EEGNet (ref-001) using BCI Competition IV's ERN dataset (ref-001), with baselines including standard SDP verification (ref-005) and Parseval networks (ref-010). Measures include certification rates, classification accuracy, and perturbation bounds under ethical constraints. Ablation studies isolate the impact of neuro-rights constraints by comparing results with/without them.

candidates.title: Adversarial Vulnerability of EEGNet Visualization Mechanisms
candidates.summary: This paper tests whether EEGNet's gradient-weighted class activation mapping (Grad-CAM) visualization technique reveals attack surfaces in BCI systems. The hypothesis is that Grad-CAM-guided perturbations achieve higher success rates with lower magnitude than random or non-visualization baselines. The approach generates targeted adversarial examples using EEGNet's Grad-CAM saliency maps and compares them to random channel masking and input gradient baselines. Evaluation measures attack success rates, perturbation L2 norms, and cross-subject/paradigm transferability on the BCI Competition IV datasets.
candidates.gap: While ref-021 and ref-024 demonstrate adversarial vulnerabilities in EEG-based BCIs, they do not isolate whether visualization techniques like Grad-CAM specifically expose attack surfaces. The closest work (ref-021) focuses on detection methods, not attack generation guided by model interpretability tools.
candidates.approach: Inputs: EEGNet model trained on BCI Competition IV datasets, test EEG trials. Outputs: Adversarial examples with minimal L2 perturbations. Objective: Maximize classification error while minimizing perturbation magnitude. Update rule: Projected gradient descent (PGD) with step size 0.01, 20 iterations. Perturbation mask: Binary mask derived from EEGNet's Grad-CAM saliency map (top 10% channels/timepoints). Difference from ref-024: Uses Grad-CAM guidance instead of universal perturbation optimization.
candidates.evaluation: Setting: BCI Competition IV P300/MRCP datasets. Baselines: (1) Random channel masking (ref-024), (2) Input gradient masking without CNN feature maps. Measures: Attack success rate (ASR), mean perturbation L2 norm. Ablation: Compare ASR/L2 for Grad-CAM-guided vs baselines under equal PGD budget. Transfer test: Evaluate perturbations on unseen subjects/paradigms. Central claim test: Higher ASR with lower L2 for Grad-CAM-guided attacks proves visualization techniques expose vulnerabilities.
